data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The nocturnal UHI is controlled by a coupling between reduced wind speed in urban canyons and the rate of stored-heat release: dense building geometry dampens nocturnal ventilation, trapping the sensible heat released from thermal mass, so the gap scales with city size and built density.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If nocturnal UHI magnitude does not correlate with wind speed reduction after controlling for thermal mass, the ventilation mechanism is not the modulator","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If open-grid cities with good ventilation but high thermal mass show the same UHI as dense canyon cities, wind speed is not the controlling factor","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the gap is independent of city size, the scaling argument fails","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the UHI is larger on windy nights than calm nights in some cities, the ventilation-trapping mechanism is contradicted","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Urban roughness and street-canyon geometry increase aerodynamic drag and reduce mean wind speed relative to open countryside. On a calm night, this reduced ventilation means that the sensible heat being released from the thermal mass of buildings and roads is not advected away but accumulates in the urban canopy layer. The cross-city modulator is the product of stored heat (proportional to impervious surface area and city size) and the inverse of ventilation rate (inversely proportional to building height and built density). Cities with taller buildings and denser street networks produce larger nocturnal UHI gaps because they both store more daytime heat and ventilate it more slowly.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
